endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Use real-time auditing tools where they can be demonstrated to aid in the tracking and validation of the lineage and authenticity of AI-generated data.

endorsements.title: The Invisible Risks of AI-Generated Health Information
endorsements.quote: We recommend that they detect, watermark, and label synthetic health content, and withhold it from wide distribution until experts have vetted it and established its provenance.

endorsements.title: The ChatGPT Effect: Nursing Education and Generative Artificial Intelligence
endorsements.quote: Clear institutional guidelines, comprehensive student education on generative AI, and tools to detect AI-generated content are recommended to navigate these challenges.

endorsements.title: Rethinking Pediatric Human-AI Interaction for Building Safer Digital Health Ecosystems
endorsements.quote: This ecosystem must include algorithmic transparency summaries that are accessible to young readers, uniform labeling of AI-generated health content, and safety protocols that monitor for misinterpretation patterns over time.

endorsements.title: Generative AI-Assisted Medical Illustrations in Pediatric Neurosurgery : Workflows, Ethical Safeguards, and Journal Policy Considerations
endorsements.quote: Provenance information should be preserved wherever technically feasible, and never deliberately removed to obscure the contribution of AI [ 11 ].

endorsements.title: Text-to-Video Generative Artificial Intelligence in Pediatrics: Potential Applications, Ethical Considerations, and Future Directions
endorsements.quote: Thus, the development of detection mechanisms and ethical frameworks is necessary for the responsible and effective implementation of these technologies [ 6 ].

endorsements.title: Ethical considerations for multimodal artificial intelligence in healthcare
endorsements.quote: We propose that provenance labeling for MMAI-generated data be treated as a foundational requirement rather than an optional transparency measure.

endorsements.title: Multilayered Epistemic Disruption in AI-Driven Health Misinformation: Conceptual Framework and Viewpoint
endorsements.quote: User-friendly tools that allow clinicians to cryptographically sign authentic content (C2PA-compatible), institutional mechanisms for health organizations to mark their digital presence as verifiable, and health literacy programs redesigned to include ecosystem awareness, teaching people to recognize coordinated information systems, not just individual false claims, all belong in this layer.

endorsements.title: AI-generated medical realism and hantavirus misinformation: a new public health threat?
endorsements.quote: Digital platforms should implement scalable monitoring systems capable of detecting and flagging AI- generated health misinformation during outbreak events, and invest in the development and integration of digital watermarking and content-authenticity verification tools to facilitate rapid identification of synthetic medical content.

evidence.title: Cross sectional pilot study on clinical review generation using large language models
evidence.outcome: Ability of current detection systems to identify AI-generated review content
evidence.effect: Current detection systems were inefficient at identifying AI-generated content; no numbers in the abstract.
evidence.quote: Moreover, the study uncovers a concerning inefficiency in current detection systems for identifying AI-generated content, suggesting a need for more advanced checking systems and a stronger ethical framework to ensure academic transparency.

evidence.title: The detectability paradox: bilingual medical report generation with open-weight models and the limits of human oversight
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.outcome: Detection of AI-generated reports by automated classifier versus human experts
evidence.effect: EuroBERT classifier achieved overall accuracy 0.98 versus experts 0.60, supporting automated detection tools for provenance.
evidence.quote: As shown in Table 3 , in contrast to human experts, the machine learning-based classifier leveraging EuroBERT 18 achieved a robust detection performance with an overall accuracy of 0.98 ( P < 0.001).
evidence.sample_unit: medical reports (100 reports rated by 9 experts)

evidence.title: Factuality Beyond Coherence: Evaluating LLM Watermarking Methods for Medical Texts
evidence.outcome: Effect of LLM watermarking (content provenance) on factual accuracy and coherence of medical text
evidence.effect: Current watermarking methods substantially compromise medical factuality, with entropy shifts degrading medical entity representation.
evidence.quote: Our evaluation shows current watermarking methods substantially compromise medical factuality, with entropy shifts degrading medical entity representation.

evidence.title: Marking the Wrong Symptoms: Evaluating LLM Watermarks in Medical Texts
evidence.outcome: Effect of watermarking (content provenance) on medical reasoning quality, terminology, hallucinations
evidence.effect: Watermarking can induce substantial degradation across failure modes, including lexical corruption, hallucinated terminology, and amplified misattribution or omission of image findings.
evidence.quote: Our results reveal that watermarking can induce substantial degradation across multiple failure modes, including lexical corruption, hallucinated terminology, and amplified misattribution or omission of image findings.
evidence.sample_unit: not reported (5 watermarking schemes across 11 LLMs and 7 VLMs on medical tasks)

evidence.title: Differentiating ChatGPT-Generated and Human-Written Medical Texts: Quantitative Study
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of machine learning detection of ChatGPT-generated versus human-written medical text
evidence.effect: A BERT-based detector identified ChatGPT-generated medical texts with an F1 score above 95%.
evidence.quote: A bidirectional encoder representations from transformers-based model effectively detected medical texts generated by ChatGPT, and the F<sub>1</sub> score exceeded 95%.

evidence.title: Prompt engineering on leveraging large language models in generating response to InBasket messages
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.outcome: Patient advisors’ ability to identify AI-generated responses when blinded to authorship
evidence.effect: Patient advisors correctly identified AI-generated responses only 24% of the time; 50% were attributed to humans, and authorship was undetermined for 26%.
evidence.quote: As shown in Figure 5 , in the final round of patient evaluation, patients determined that 77% ( N = 192) of responses completely addressed patient questions, and patients correctly identified messages were AI-generated only 24% of the time.

evidence.title: Non-contrast CT synthesis using patch-based cycle-consistent generative adversarial network (Cycle-GAN) for radiomics and deep learning in the era of COVID-19
evidence.outcome: Expert ability to distinguish synthetic from acquired CT images in modified Turing test
evidence.effect: Human experts misclassified synthetic images with a false positive rate of 67% and Fleiss' Kappa 0.06, so synthetic images were not reliably distinguishable from acquired ones.
evidence.quote: In a modified Turing-test, human experts identified synthetic vs acquired images, with a false positive rate of 67% and Fleiss' Kappa 0.06, attesting to the photorealism of the synthetic images.

evidence.title: Comparing the Ability of Google and ChatGPT to Accurately Respond to Oculoplastics-Related Patient Questions and Generate Customized Oculoplastics Patient Education Materials
evidence.outcome: Expert identification of AI-generated FAQ responses
evidence.effect: Among panelists making a choice, 31% (38/121) correctly identified the AI-generated response.
evidence.quote: Of the panelists who elected to make a selection, 31% (38/121) correctly identified the AI-generated response ( Table 5 ).
evidence.sample_unit: patient FAQs (10 oculoplastics conditions) plus 8 procedure explanations

evidence.title: Comparing the Accuracy and Readability of Glaucoma-related Question Responses and Educational Materials by Google and ChatGPT
evidence.effect: Experts correctly identified AI-generated FAQ responses 39.5% (34/86).
evidence.quote: Among the responses that experts attempted to identify, 39.5% (34/86) were correctly identified as the AI-generated response ( Table 5 ).

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence-generated podcasts open new doors to make science accessible: a mixed-method evaluation of quality and the potential for science communication
evidence.outcome: Participants' ability to identify podcasts as AI-generated when not told
evidence.effect: Only half of participants were able to identify the AI nature of the podcasts when not informed beforehand.
evidence.quote: Only half of them were able to identify this aspect.

evidence.title: Human perception of AI-generated post-treatment orthodontic facial images: factors associated with misclassification
evidence.outcome: Participants' ability to distinguish AI-enhanced from real post-treatment orthodontic images
evidence.effect: 63.2% misclassified AI-enhanced images as real; 18.5% misclassified real images as AI-generated; higher trust in AI content increased odds of misclassification (OR 1.38).
evidence.quote: A total of 63.2% of participants misclassified AI-enhanced images as real, whereas 18.5% misclassified real images as AI-generated.

evidence.title: Rethinking Pediatric Asthma Education Through Large Language Model Generation and Simplification: Randomized Double-Blind Study
evidence.outcome: source identification accuracy for AI-generated materials
evidence.effect: Only 7.3% (25/344) in the LLM groups correctly identified materials as LLM-generated, while 80.6% (141/175) in the expert group recognized human-authored content.
evidence.quote: While 80.6% (141/175) of participants in the PEARs group accurately recognized published expert-authored content, merely 7.3% (25/344) in the AI-generated groups correctly identified the content as LLM-generated.

evidence.title: Blind spots in artificial intelligence systems: poor identification of self-generated medical images-evidence-based cross-sectional study
evidence.outcome: Ability of AI models to identify their own generated medical images as AI-generated
evidence.effect: 27/32 incorrect vs 5/32 correct (84.37% vs 15.62%; p = 0.001); ChatGPT accuracy 18.75%, Gemini 12.5%; Gemini anatomy images 0% correct.
evidence.quote: There were significantly higher incorrect rates than correct identification rates for AI-generated images overall (27/32 incorrect vs. 5/32 correct; 84.37% vs. 15.62%; p = 0.001).
evidence.sample_unit: AI-generated medical images identification attempts (16 images x 2 models)

commentary.bottom_line: Five offline or benchmark studies test parts of this practice: two detection classifiers report high accuracy, one study finds detection systems inefficient, and two benchmarks find that watermarking degrades medical text. No study tests whether labels or provenance tracking help clinicians or patients judge authenticity in real use.

perspectives.view: All five tests are level 4 or 5 designs in offline or benchmark settings, and none measures a user or patient outcome. The detector studies disagree, with one classifier reaching accuracy 0.98 and another an F1 above 95%, while a third study found detection inefficient. Indirectness, inconsistency, and design limits support very low certainty.

Two benchmarks report that watermarking can introduce hallucinated terminology, lexical corruption, and misattributed image findings in medical text. The provenance mechanism itself may therefore create a new route for errors to reach clinicians. A hazard study found experts misclassified synthetic CT images with a 67% false positive rate, but it does not show that labels would prevent this.

In a Swiss simulation, an automated classifier reached accuracy 0.98 on medical reports, compared with 0.60 for nine experts. This suggests tools may outperform human review. No study reports how detection or labeling fits into clinical workflows. None addresses alert burden or the handling of false positives in live systems.

The Swiss detection study included non-English medical reports. A Chinese randomized trial found that only 7.3% of participants identified LLM-generated materials. No test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy groups, and these groups may depend most on labels they can read and interpret.

NIST AI 600-1 conditions its guidance on auditing tools that can be demonstrated to aid lineage and authenticity tracking. The current evidence shows mixed detector performance and, in benchmarks, watermarking harms to medical factuality. This evidence may not yet meet that demonstration condition for clinical content.

In a real deployment dataset, patient advisors identified AI-generated responses 24% of the time and attributed 50% to humans. Patients may therefore not know when a machine wrote a message to them. No study tested whether a label changes patient trust or understanding, or whether it affects patients' ability to reach a clinician.

commentary.research_gap: No study deploys labeling or provenance tracking in live patient portals or clinical documentation. Such studies should measure whether users correctly judge authenticity, whether trust and reliance change, and whether watermarking alters the factual accuracy of clinical text. They should also report detector false-positive rates on human-written content and enroll diverse patient populations.
commentary.underserved_note: One detection test (pmid:42097830) included non-English medical reports, but no test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations. No evidence shows whether patients with limited literacy or limited English proficiency understand content labels, so effects in those groups cannot be inferred.
